MESSAGE:
Need a hand with our quarterly marketing report, it's due Friday and I'm behind.

First, give me a better title than "Q3 Marketing Report", ideally something that signals it's about what actually worked. Second, what chart type would you use to show monthly signups across three channels over the quarter? Also define "bounce rate" in one line for the execs, and suggest three questions they're likely to ask so I can prep answers.

Landing page A got 2,000 visits and converted at 10%. Landing page B got 200 visits and converted at 30%. In the summary slide I was going to write "overall conversion rate across both pages was 20%". Is that the right figure to report? If not, what is it?

Should the detailed appendix tables go at the back of the slide deck or in a separate spreadsheet that I link to? Our CFO likes to dig into numbers but the CEO hates long decks, so I'm a bit torn on that one. Whatever you suggest, I'll need to defend it in the meeting.

Thanks, you're a lifesaver. I'll be working through all of these tonight and tomorrow morning.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a better report title
2. Recommend a chart type for monthly signups across three channels
3. Define 'bounce rate' in one line
4. Suggest three likely exec questions
5. Check the 20% overall conversion figure and give the correct one  KEY: 20% is wrong (it is an unweighted average of two rates). Pooled rate = (200 + 60) / (2,000 + 200) = 260 / 2,200 = about 11.8%. Must report ~11.8%.
6. Recommend appendix tables in the deck vs a separate spreadsheet

ANSWER:
Here's everything, in order.

## 1. Title options

- **"Q3 Marketing: What Worked and Where We're Doubling Down"**
- **"Q3 Results: The Channels and Pages That Delivered"**
- **"What Moved the Needle in Q3"**

The first one is the strongest. It signals results and also points to next steps, which executives usually care about most.

## 2. Chart for monthly signups across three channels

I'd use a **clustered column chart**, with months on the x-axis and one coloured bar per channel in each month.

With only three months, a line chart has just three points per line, which looks thin. Columns make it easy to compare channels within each month and to see the month-to-month change. Use the same colour for each channel throughout the deck, and label the bars with values if the CEO prefers to see numbers at a glance.

If one channel is clearly growing and that's your main story, a **line chart** with that line highlighted would also work.

## 3. Bounce rate in one line

> **Bounce rate is the percentage of visitors who land on a page and leave without taking any further action, such as clicking or viewing another page.**

If you use Google Analytics 4, it defines bounce rate slightly differently: the share of sessions that weren't "engaged," meaning under 10 seconds, no conversion and only one page viewed. Have that ready in case someone asks why the numbers look different from older reports.

## 4. Questions the executives are likely to ask

1. **"What did each channel cost per signup, and which gives us the best return?"** Have cost per acquisition by channel ready, not just volumes.
2. **"Landing page B converts at 30%, so why aren't we sending all our traffic there?"** See the note on sample size below.
3. **"What are we changing in Q4 because of this, and what do we need from the budget?"** They'll want the decision, not just the data.

Other likely questions are how this compares with Q2 or last year's Q3, and whether these signups turn into paying customers.

## 5. Overall conversion rate: not 20%

20% is the simple average of 10% and 30%, but the two pages had very different traffic. The overall rate has to be **weighted by visits**:

| Page | Visits | Conversion rate | Conversions |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2,000 | 10% | 200 |
| B | 200 | 30% | 60 |
| **Total** | **2,200** | | **260** |

**Overall conversion rate = 260 ÷ 2,200 = 11.8%**

Report **11.8%**. Writing 20% would overstate performance by about two-thirds, and a CFO who likes to dig into numbers may spot it.

Present page B carefully as well. Its 30% comes from only 200 visits, so it's promising but less certain than page A's figure. A good way to phrase it is "B is a strong early signal worth testing with more traffic," which also prepares you for question 2.

## 6. Appendix: back of the deck or a separate spreadsheet?

I'd recommend a **linked spreadsheet**, plus **one backup slide** at the end of the deck.

- **The main deck** stays short for the CEO and covers only results and decisions.
- **One backup slide** after the closing slide holds a compact table of the key figures: signups, cost and conversions by channel. That way you can answer the CFO's most likely questions during the meeting without switching files.
- **The full detail goes in the spreadsheet,** linked from the backup slide and sent beforehand so the CFO can review it at their own pace.

To defend it in the meeting, you could say:

> "I've kept the deck to the decisions we need to make. All the underlying numbers are in the linked spreadsheet, which I sent round yesterday, and there's a backup slide with the key figures if we want to go into detail now."

That respects the CEO's time, gives the CFO more detail than slides could hold, and shows you've planned for both.

Good luck with the report.
